title: Evaluation, calibration & experimental design
summary: Make model comparisons that survive contact with real data and actual decisions.
html:
Make model comparisons that survive contact with real data and actual decisions.

How the pieces connect

Separate fitting from selection

Use training data to fit parameters, validation data to choose models and thresholds, and a held-out test for the final comparison. Repeatedly optimizing against a test set effectively turns it into validation data. Cross-validation helps estimate variability, provided folds respect groups and time.

Metrics answer different questions

Precision asks how many predicted positives were positive. Recall asks how many actual positives were found. PR curves are often informative for rare events. AUROC evaluates ranking across thresholds but can look strong while precision is poor. For regression, MAE and RMSE penalize errors differently.

Calibrated confidence

Among predictions near 0.8, calibration asks whether roughly 80% are correct under the specified event definition. Reliability diagrams, Brier score, and log loss help assess probability quality. Recalibration uses held-out data and can fail under distribution shift.

Measure the system and its slices

Report sample counts, uncertainty, baselines, and important subgroups. Paired comparisons on the same examples can reduce variance. Online experiments need assignment units that avoid interference. Evaluate fallback behavior, cost, response time, and human correction work alongside model quality.

Worked example

A classifier yields 80 true positives, 20 false positives, and 40 false negatives. Precision=80/100=0.80; recall=80/120≈0.667; F1≈0.727. Neither metric alone says whether the system is acceptable without error costs and population context.

What goes wrong

An improvement smaller than run-to-run variation may be noise. Selecting the best of many trials without accounting for selection makes gains look more reliable than they are.

Check your understanding

Why is a customer-grouped split sometimes better than a random row split?

Reveal the explanation

It tests generalization to new customers rather than recognition of repeated patterns from customers already seen in training.

An operating model for evaluation, calibration & experimental design

Evaluation is an experiment design problem. The test set estimates behavior under the world your split represents. If deployment is temporal, grouped, adversarial, multilingual, or costly, a random aggregate score cannot answer the whole question. Measurement needs to follow the actual decision path.

The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test.

Worked system: the aggregate score that conceals a release failure

An assistant scores 92% on a mixed evaluation set. Broken down by language, document age, and question type, it may be 98% on common English requests, 71% on a supported language, and near zero on requests requiring a current internal policy. The aggregate is mathematically correct but operationally incomplete. A user experiences a slice, a task, and a consequence—not the weighted average.

Define a release scorecard before tuning: baseline, split rule, sample counts, confidence interval or repeated-run variance, important slices, latency, cost, abstention behavior, and known exclusions. Keep the test set separate from the examples used to select prompts or thresholds. Evaluation becomes useful when it can veto a release for a reason a user would recognize.

Notebook: Measure the decision boundary, not only accuracy

Create an evaluation card for every release: data version, split rule, sample size, baselines, metric definitions, confidence intervals, slices, latency, cost, and known blind spots.

from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix
tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred).ravel()
precision = tp / (tp + fp)
recall = tp / (tp + fn)
print({"precision": precision, "recall": recall})
What to test next. 1. Specify outcome: Name the user decision and target population. 2. Design split: Protect held-out data from all selection steps. 3. Measure: Use metrics, uncertainty, and slices. 4. Decide: Compare against baseline and operational constraints.

The gotcha. A small inspection script proves only the quantities it prints. Preserve units, shapes, versions, and the input fixture beside its output.

A rigorous way to practice

  1. Specify outcome. Name the user decision and target population.
  2. Design split. Protect held-out data from all selection steps.
  3. Measure. Use metrics, uncertainty, and slices.
  4. Decide. Compare against baseline and operational constraints.

Create an evaluation card for every release: data version, split rule, sample size, baselines, metric definitions, confidence intervals, slices, latency, cost, and known blind spots.

Verification questions for evaluation, calibration & experimental design

BoundaryQuestionEvidence
Specify outcomeWhat would show that this boundary failed?Name the user decision and target population.
Design splitWhat would show that this boundary failed?Protect held-out data from all selection steps.
MeasureWhat would show that this boundary failed?Use metrics, uncertainty, and slices.
DecideWhat would show that this boundary failed?Compare against baseline and operational constraints.

The gotcha. Passing each component check separately does not prove the composed path preserves identity, units, ordering, or authority.

An evaluation is an experiment with a release decision

The dataset, sampling frame, protocol, metric, baseline, uncertainty, and veto rule jointly define what an evaluation can support.

  • Protect the test set from selection. Prompt tuning, checkpoint choice, feature design, and repeated error inspection all adapt to examples.
  • Report denominators and intervals. A slice score without sample count can turn one example into a confident-looking percentage.
  • Measure the operating point. Calibration, threshold errors, abstention, latency, cost, and human escalation connect model scores to a service.
  • Use counterexamples and shifts. Aggregate IID accuracy misses temporal change, adversarial inputs, unsupported requests, and rare high-cost errors.

The gotcha. A benchmark can be measured perfectly and still lack construct validity for the claimed capability.
